summary.text: Pell's equation is a Diophantine equation of the form x² − ny² = 1, where n is a given positive nonsquare integer and integer solutions are sought for x and y.
Lagrange proved that when n is not a perfect square there are infinitely many distinct whole-number solutions.
Those solutions give fractions x/y that closely approximate the square root of n.

facts.label: Odd naming
facts.value: Euler wrongly credited Brouncker's solution to John Pell

facts.label: Its graph
facts.value: A hyperbola, with solutions at whole-number points

facts.value: His cattle problem can be recast as a Pell's equation

items.prompt: People call this equation by Pell's name, yet John Pell did not solve it first in Europe. How did the name arise?

options.label: Pell wrote the first European textbook on the topic
Euler mistakenly credited Brouncker's solution to Pell
Brouncker named it after his teacher, John Pell
Lagrange renamed it to honour a rival of Fermat

items.explain: William Brouncker was the first European to solve it, but Leonhard Euler mistakenly attributed Brouncker's solution to John Pell, and the name stuck.

items.prompt: You need a fraction made of whole numbers that sits very close to the square root of a non-square number. How can this equation help?

options.label: Its whole-number solutions x and y give fractions x/y that approximate the root
It lists the digits of the root one at a time
It proves the root can be written exactly as a fraction
It shows which roots are impossible to approximate

items.explain: Solutions can be used to approximate the square root of n accurately by rational numbers of the form x/y.

items.prompt: A student finds one nontrivial solution for a given n that is not a perfect square and assumes that is the only one. What is true?

options.label: There is exactly one more, found by swapping x and y
The one found is the only solution
There are only a handful, and none for large x
There are endlessly many distinct solutions, as Lagrange proved

items.explain: Lagrange proved that as long as n is not a perfect square, the equation has infinitely many distinct integer solutions.

items.prompt: The equation is drawn as a curve on a grid. What does a solution look like on that picture?

options.label: Any point where the curve crosses the horizontal axis
Any point along the curve, since each one satisfies the equation
A point on the curve whose two coordinates are both whole numbers
The highest point of the curve

items.explain: The equation is a hyperbola, and solutions occur where the curve passes through a point whose x and y coordinates are both integers.

items.prompt: An ancient word problem asks how many cattle belong to the sun god Helios. How can it be solved?

options.label: By rewriting it as a Pell's equation
By counting the herd in a single field
By drawing a hyperbola and measuring it
It has never been solved by any method

items.explain: Archimedes's cattle problem can be solved by reformulating it as a Pell's equation.

items.prompt: The Pythagoreans used 'side' and 'diameter' number pairs x and y. What did the ratio x/y approximate?

options.label: The square root of 3
The number pi
The golden ratio
The square root of 2

items.explain: If x and y are positive integers satisfying the equation for n = 2, then x/y approximates the square root of 2, and the Pythagoreans knew these side and diameter numbers.
